title: POC Weekly Sync - Throughput Optimization
summary: Weekly POC sync to review throughput test results, adjust batching and concurrency targets, and agree next steps for benchmark runs. Key focus: continuous batching parameters, target concurrency, queue depth and warmup behavior. Decided to increase concurrency caps, tune batching window from 25ms -> 15ms for short-seq traffic, and run multi-day steady-state test with traffic replay.
next_steps: Redwood to share updated perf dashboard & config diff by EOD Thursday
BrightScale to provide production traffic replay logs (anonymized) by Monday
Schedule 48-hour steady-state benchmark for next Wednesday
SE run guidance doc for batching window + concurrency knobs
action_items: Priya Shah - produce config diff and perf dashboard snapshot (due 2025-08-14)
Samir Gupta - share anonymized traffic replay and seq len distribution (due 2025-08-18)
Alex Morgan - send pricing implications for increased concurrency and Dedicated prewarm (due 2025-08-16)
Rina Patel - confirm target SLA for tail latency and acceptable p99 (due 2025-08-15)
transcript:
[00:00:00] Alex Morgan: All right, everyone, good afternoon. thanks for joining, we'll kick off the weekly POC sync. agenda is quick results review and tuning decisions for throughput.
[00:00:12] Aisha Osman: thanks Alex, quick note we have the usual folks from BrightScale on, Carlos, Rina, Samir. we'll keep to an hour.
[00:00:22] Priya Shah: Hey team, i pulled up last night's run - the steady-state for the 4 GPU pool on the dedicated instance. i have a dashboard link in the chat, but quick headline: sustained 1.1M tokens/min with avg latency ~210ms, p95 ~480ms, p99 ~890ms. batch size distribution skewed: median batch ~18 tokens, mean ~24, and there's a long tail from bursts.
[00:00:48] Carlos Mendoza: ok that's helpful. our target for production is 1.5M tokens/min and p99 < 1s. looks like we're getting close on throughput but p99 is creeping.
[00:00:59] Priya Shah: yes, exactly. we dug into the logs and saw two things: first, the batching window was set to 25ms for this run which favors latency but reduces batch packing for our traffic because a lot of requests are short sequences (avg seq len 32). second, we hit queue depth spikes when concurrent request bursts exceed the concurrency cap, which forces the runtime to form smaller batches and stalls some requests.
[00:01:28] Rina Patel: can you explain the queue depth spike bit? is that backpressure inside the runtime?
[00:01:33] Priya Shah: yeah so the runtime maintains a request queue per worker and a concurrency cap controls how many requests can be in flight to the GPU. when we hit a sudden burst, requests wait in the queue until a GPU slot opens; if the batching window is short we end up sending many small batches instead of one medium batch which hurts GPU utilization and increases p99.
[00:01:53] Samir Gupta: is the KV cache hit ratio affecting this? since we have many repeated prefixes in requests, i expected higher cache reuse.
[00:01:59] Jon Park: good question. KV cache warmup looks fine for longer sessions but the traffic pattern is lots of single-turn requests so KV hits are low in this workload. we did enable prefix caching but for these short sequences the overhead of managing many small KV lookups add to tail.
[00:02:15] Priya Shah: recommendation: for short-seq heavy traffic, reduce batching window to 10-15ms and raise concurrency cap by 20%-30% to allow the runtime to aggregate more requests before the window fires; also increase the max queue depth threshold to avoid dropping into many tiny batches under bursts.
[00:02:34] Carlos Mendoza: Raising concurrency sounds like it might raise latency for some requests and also cost. what's the tradeoff?
[00:02:39] Alex Morgan: yep tradeoff is cost vs latency vs throughput. in our internal tests raising concurrency increased sustained tokens/min by ~25% and improved p99 in steady-state because GPUs are fuller, but tail can spike if you don't tune the batching window and queueing. we'll show cost delta in the pricing note.
[00:02:55] Rina Patel: any risk to stability? we can't have unbounded memory growth at the worker if we increase concurrency and queue depth.
[00:03:03] Priya Shah: absolutely, you cap memory usage on the workers. we recommend incremental increases and monitoring worker memory and OOM counters; also we can enable a soft admission control that starts shedding non-critical low-priority requests if memory crosses a threshold.
[00:03:15] Aisha Osman: can you walk through the specific config values you'd want to test?
[00:03:19] Priya Shah: sure — for the next run I propose: batching_window_ms = 15, concurrency_per_worker = 32 (was 24), max_queue_depth = 128 (was 64), batch_size_cap = 256 tokens. also enable adaptive batching with a 30s warmup phase.
[00:03:36] Samir Gupta: how does adaptive batching differ from continuous batching?
[00:03:40] Jon Park: continuous batching is where the runtime continuously aggregates requests into the KV/cache-aware pipeline; adaptive batching will dynamically vary the window based on observed arrival rates and seq length distribution. adaptive can help during mixed traffic where sometimes you want larger windows.
[00:03:57] Carlos Mendoza: do we have telemetry on queueing behavior per worker so we can validate these changes?
[00:04:02] Priya Shah: yes dashboard has per-worker queue length, batch size distribution, GPU utilization and per-request queuing time. i'll pull snapshots after the run.
[00:04:10] Alex Morgan: quick note on warmup — the first 10-15 minutes of a run often show lower throughput due to KV cache and kernel warmup. for production you should plan for a prewarm traffic injection. Dedicated prewarm options are available which hold warmed workers for a small cost.
[00:04:25] Rina Patel: that might be important; our SLA budget can't degrade during business hours. what's the expected cost of a prewarm?
[00:04:30] Alex Morgan: i'll send a short pricing calc, but rough ballpark for holding two warm workers is about 7-10% of the committed pool hourly. exact depends on model size and number of GPUs.
[00:04:43] Samir Gupta: regarding the kernel selection — we saw some variance on latency between runs; is that from mixed quantized kernels?
[00:04:50] Priya Shah: yep the runtime picks kernels based on seq len and hardware capabilities; if a request crosses a threshold it may pick a different execution path. we can force consistent kernel selection for the benchmark to isolate that variable.
[00:05:03] Carlos Mendoza: good idea, let's lock kernel selection for the next steady-state test.
[00:05:06] Aisha Osman: any other tuning recommendations?
[00:05:08] Priya Shah: also recommend enabling request coalescing for identical prompts at the front where feasible; and set a retry policy with jitter for transient queuing failures so clients back off a bit instead of immediate retries.
[00:05:19] Rina Patel: about retries — we saw retries create thundering herd during one of our smaller tests. a jittered exponential backoff should help.
[00:05:26] Jon Park: also consider shaping incoming traffic with a token bucket at the proxy layer so spikes are smoothed before they hit the runtime. that reduced max queue length in our other customers by 40%.
[00:05:38] Samir Gupta: ok sounds actionable. for the next run we will provide a 24-hour traffic replay that mirrors our prod daytime pattern. you recommended anonymized logs?
[00:05:46] Priya Shah: yes anonymized is fine, we only need timestamps, seq length, and arrival rates; no PII.
[00:05:52] Alex Morgan: timeline then: BrightScale to send anonymized replay by Monday, Redwood will update config and run a 48-hour steady-state on Wed-Thu next week; results shared in follow up.
[00:06:03] Carlos Mendoza: can you annotate the dashboard with which timestamps correspond to config changes and kernel locks? that will help correlate.
[00:06:09] Priya Shah: yes we'll include annotated markers.
[00:06:12] Aisha Osman: any concerns about the KV cache and our repeated prefixes? i want to make sure we don't over-optimize for very short sequences and then regress on medium-length ones.
[00:06:22] Jon Park: fair point. the plan with adaptive batching and keeping a slightly elevated concurrency cap is to be robust across lengths; we'll also run a mixed-benchmark with 20/60/20 short/medium/long sequences.
[00:06:35] Rina Patel: what's the expected improvement in p99 if we implement these changes?
[00:06:38] Priya Shah: based on similar customers we'd expect p99 to drop from ~890ms to around 600-700ms while throughput increases ~20-30%, assuming steady arrival rate. but worst-case spikes can still occur if there's an extreme burst and prewarm isn't used.
[00:06:52] Samir Gupta: fine for us as long as SLA p99 under 1s holds.
[00:06:56] Alex Morgan: final checklist: lock kernels for bench, apply config diff (window=15ms, concurrency=32, queue=128), enable adaptive batching and annotated dashboard, run 48hr bench, share results.
[00:07:10] Aisha Osman: sounds good. one last thing — can you capture cost delta for both hosted and dedicated options for these changes? we might move to Dedicated if the economics work.
[00:07:19] Alex Morgan: will do.
[00:07:21] Priya Shah: i'll attach the config diff and sample monitor snapshots after this call.
[00:07:26] Carlos Mendoza: thanks everyone. we'll get the replay to you.
[00:07:29] Alex Morgan: thanks team — meeting adjourned.
[00:07:33] 
[00:07:33] (Post-call quick notes)
[00:07:35] Priya Shah: NOTE: during the run we observed occasional small packetization artifacts in transcripts — transcription engine mislabels 'KV' as 'kev' in some logs, please ignore.
notes: Decided to test smaller batching window and higher concurrency; run 48-hr benchmark with locked kernels and anonymized traffic replay. Pricing and config diffs to follow; prewarm discussed as mitigation for warmup tail.
